title: NJ Driver's Manual – Chapter 6
subtitle: Sharing the Road
note: Based on the 2025 NJ Driver's Manual, Chapter 6. Verify all answers against the current manual before your exam.

questions.q: NJ law requires a minimum clearance of how many feet when passing a bicyclist?
opts: 1 foot
2 feet
3 feet
5 feet
questions.exp: NJ's '3-Foot Passing Law' requires drivers to give cyclists at least 3 feet of lateral clearance when passing. If the road is too narrow, wait until it is safe to pass with that clearance.

questions.q: When a bicyclist is riding in the travel lane, they:
opts: Must move onto the sidewalk when one is available
Are entitled to the full width of the travel lane and must be given the same rights as other vehicles
Must stay within 3 feet of the curb at all times
Are required to dismount at intersections
questions.exp: Cyclists have the same rights and duties as motor vehicle drivers. They may use the full lane and do not have to move to the right edge just because a car is behind them.

questions.q: Before making a right turn across a bicycle lane, you must:
opts: Sound your horn to alert any cyclist
Use your high beams to increase visibility
Yield to any cyclist already in or approaching the bicycle lane
Park in the bike lane briefly to check for cyclists
questions.exp: When turning right across a bike lane, yield to cyclists in the lane. Signal early, check mirrors and blind spots, then merge into the bike lane (where permitted) and complete the turn.

questions.q: A driver must yield to pedestrians:
opts: Only at marked crosswalks with traffic signals
Only if the pedestrian has already stepped off the curb
At all crosswalks — marked or unmarked — when pedestrians are crossing or about to cross
Only during school hours in school zones
questions.exp: NJ law requires drivers to yield at all crosswalks — marked or unmarked. An unmarked crosswalk exists at every intersection where a sidewalk meets the road.

questions.q: Motorcycles are entitled to:
opts: Share a lane side-by-side with a car
The full width of a traffic lane, just as a car would be
Ride only on the right one-third of the lane
Use the shoulder to pass slow traffic
questions.exp: A motorcyclist is entitled to the full width of their lane. Do not attempt to share a lane with a motorcycle or crowd them to the side.

questions.q: When following a motorcycle, you should:
opts: Follow at the same distance you would a car
Follow more closely so you can see their brake lights clearly
Maintain a larger following distance than with a car — motorcycles can stop quickly and their brake lights may be harder to see
Flash your high beams to signal your presence
questions.exp: Motorcycles can stop much faster than cars. Maintain a following distance of at least 4 seconds behind a motorcycle. Also, their brake lights are small and easy to miss.

questions.q: When following a large truck, you should increase your following distance primarily because:
opts: Trucks accelerate and brake faster than cars
The truck obstructs your forward view, and trucks need far more stopping distance
Trucks create heavy wind turbulence at close range
It is required by federal law
questions.exp: Large trucks block your view of the road and traffic ahead. A greater following distance gives you an earlier view around the truck and allows more time to react to the truck's braking.

questions.q: A large truck's rear blind spot ('No Zone') extends approximately how far behind the trailer?
opts: 10 feet
30 feet
500 feet
questions.exp: The rear No Zone extends roughly 100–200 feet directly behind a large truck or trailer. If you cannot see the truck driver's face in their mirrors, you are in their blind spot.

questions.q: The danger of a truck making a 'wide right turn' is that:
opts: The truck swings wide and may hit your windshield
The truck must swing left first before turning right, potentially crushing a vehicle on its right side
The truck blocks two lanes during the turn
The truck's rear view is obstructed
questions.exp: Large trucks need extra space and often swing left before turning right. Never try to squeeze between a turning truck and the curb — the rear of the trailer can crush your vehicle.

questions.q: If you cannot see a truck driver's face in their side mirror, it means:
opts: Their mirrors are not properly adjusted
You are traveling at an unsafe speed
You are in the truck's blind spot and the driver cannot see you
The truck's mirrors are dirty
questions.exp: The rule of thumb for trucks: if you can't see the driver's face in their mirror, they can't see you. Either increase your following distance (move back) or pass completely through the blind spot quickly.

questions.q: On a road without a raised median, when must you stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and the stop arm extended?
opts: Only if you are directly behind the bus
Only if you are within 100 feet of the bus
Traffic in both directions must stop
Only if children are visibly crossing the road
questions.exp: On undivided roads (no physical barrier between lanes), all traffic in both directions must stop when a school bus displays flashing red lights and the stop arm is extended.

questions.q: On a divided highway with a physical barrier (median), when a school bus stops, which vehicles must stop?
opts: All vehicles in both directions
Only vehicles in the same direction as the bus, behind it
Only vehicles directly adjacent to the bus
No vehicles are required to stop on a divided highway
questions.exp: On a divided highway with a physical barrier, only vehicles traveling in the same direction as the bus and behind it must stop. Traffic on the other side of the barrier may continue.

questions.q: How far from a stopped school bus (with flashing red lights) must drivers stop?
opts: 10 feet
15 feet
25 feet
50 feet
questions.exp: You must stop at least 25 feet from a school bus with flashing red lights and the stop arm extended. This gives children a safe distance to cross in front of or behind the bus.

questions.q: When may you proceed past a stopped school bus with red lights flashing?
opts: When no children are visible crossing
After waiting 10 seconds
When the flashing lights stop and the stop arm is fully withdrawn
When the bus driver waves you on
questions.exp: Proceed only after the red lights have stopped flashing and the stop arm is fully withdrawn. Even then, proceed slowly and carefully — children may still be near the road.

questions.q: A pedestrian using a white cane or guide dog must be given:
opts: The right of way only at signalized intersections
The same rights as any other pedestrian
An absolute right of way — drivers must always yield
Priority only in school zones and hospital areas
questions.exp: NJ law grants persons who are blind or visually impaired (identified by a white cane or guide dog) an absolute right of way at crosswalks and intersections. Failure to yield carries stiff penalties.

questions.q: When you see pedestrians waiting at or stepping into a crosswalk, you must:
opts: Honk to let them know you are approaching
Flash your headlights so they know to wait
Slow down and stop — yield to all pedestrians in or entering a crosswalk
Proceed if no signal indicates they may cross
questions.exp: NJ law requires drivers to stop and remain stopped for pedestrians in or entering a crosswalk. Do not proceed until all pedestrians have completely crossed your half of the roadway.

questions.q: When an emergency vehicle with lights and siren approaches from any direction, you must:
opts: Speed up to clear the road quickly
Stop wherever you are immediately
Pull as far to the right as possible and stop until the vehicle has passed
Only yield if the emergency vehicle is in your lane
questions.exp: When an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and siren, immediately pull as far right as safely possible and stop. Remain stopped until the vehicle has fully passed.

questions.q: NJ's Move Over Law requires drivers approaching a stationary emergency or service vehicle with lights flashing on the shoulder to:
opts: Stop completely until the vehicle moves
Speed up to pass the scene quickly
Move over one lane away from the vehicle if safe to do so; if not, slow down significantly
Activate your own hazard lights and maintain speed
questions.exp: The Move Over Law applies to police, fire, EMS, tow trucks, and highway maintenance vehicles. Move over a lane (if safe) or slow to a speed safe for conditions. Fines are substantial.

questions.q: A driver following a police-escorted funeral procession should:
opts: Pass the procession if a gap appears
Merge into the procession if they are going the same way
Not join a moving funeral procession; yield to it at intersections even if the light is green
Activate hazard lights and drive between procession vehicles
questions.exp: Do not join or cut through a funeral procession. At intersections, yield even if your light turns green — the procession has the right to proceed together.

questions.q: When you encounter a horse and rider on the road, you should:
opts: Sound your horn to alert the rider
Maintain your normal speed and give a wide berth
Slow down significantly, pass wide, and avoid sudden movements, loud noises, or bright lights
Flash your headlights as a warning
questions.exp: Horses can spook easily and unpredictably. Slow well down, pass at a walk-speed and as far away as safely possible, avoid horns or loud acceleration, and check behind you to ensure the rider is stable.

questions.q: When you see farm equipment or a slow-moving vehicle with an orange triangle reflector ahead, you should:
opts: Pass immediately — the triangle means it is legal to pass
Assume it will pull over and maintain your speed
Slow down well in advance, follow at a safe distance, and pass only when the lane is clear and safe
Use your high beams to signal the operator to yield
questions.exp: The orange slow-moving vehicle (SMV) triangle indicates a vehicle traveling under 25 mph. Slow down early — farm equipment moves slowly and can be very wide. Pass only when completely safe.

questions.q: Motorcyclists often shift their lane position within their lane in order to:
opts: Intimidate or challenge other drivers
Ride two abreast legally
Maintain visibility, avoid road hazards, and be seen by other drivers
Signal that they are about to change lanes
questions.exp: Motorcyclists adjust their position within the lane to maximize their visibility to other drivers (especially in mirrors and blind spots), to avoid debris, and to improve sight distances at intersections and curves.

questions.q: Why should you NOT follow a motorcycle too closely?
opts: It is always illegal
Motorcycles can stop much faster than cars; also, their brake lights are small and easy to miss
Motorcycles are slower than cars and you would be impeding traffic
You must allow for the motorcycle's wind turbulence
questions.exp: Motorcycles have excellent braking capability and can stop in a shorter distance than most cars. If you tailgate, you may rear-end a motorcyclist who brakes for a small hazard you didn't see.

questions.q: When opening your vehicle door while parked, you should:
opts: Open it quickly to minimize time in traffic
Open it automatically — there is no legal obligation
Check your mirror and physically look behind you before opening — cyclists can be struck by a door ('dooring')
Only check if you are on a dedicated bicycle-lane road
questions.exp: 'Dooring' (opening a car door into an approaching cyclist) causes serious injuries. Always use the 'Dutch reach' — open the door with the hand farthest from the door, naturally turning your body to check behind you.

questions.q: If you are being tailgated by another driver, the safest response is to:
opts: Brake suddenly to force the tailgater to back off
Speed up to create more distance in front of you
Gradually slow down, creating more space ahead so you can brake more gradually if needed
Change lanes abruptly to get away from the tailgater
questions.exp: Create more buffer ahead of you. This allows you to brake more gradually (giving the tailgater time to react) and makes the lane clear for the tailgater to pass. Do not retaliate — it escalates danger.

questions.q: Children are especially vulnerable pedestrians because they:
opts: Walk faster than adults and harder to predict
Often dart into traffic unpredictably and have limited ability to judge vehicle speed and distance
Always walk in groups that block traffic
Ignore traffic signals
questions.exp: Children lack the cognitive development to reliably judge vehicle speed and gaps. They act impulsively and may dart into traffic without looking. Always slow down near schools, playgrounds, and residential areas.

questions.q: Near a school building, playground, or anywhere children are present, you should:
opts: Sound your horn to alert them of your presence
Flash your lights so they see you
Slow down significantly and be prepared to stop for any child at any time
Maintain the posted speed limit — that was set for safety
questions.exp: When children are visible anywhere near the road, reduce speed well below the posted limit and cover the brake. Children can move into the road instantly and without warning.

questions.q: The best position in which to pass a large truck is:
opts: Slowly — lingering alongside the truck to be safe
Quickly — move through the truck's blind zones without lingering
On the right side of the truck
As close to the truck as possible to minimize lane-change time
questions.exp: Pass trucks as quickly (but safely) as possible. The longer you are alongside a large truck, the longer you are in its blind spot. Signal, accelerate, and complete the pass decisively.

questions.q: A bicycle lane may be entered by a motor vehicle:
opts: Only if no cyclist is visible
Never — motor vehicles are fully prohibited from bike lanes at all times
To prepare for a right turn (entering only for the minimum necessary distance) or to enter/exit a driveway
Only in an emergency
questions.exp: You may briefly enter a bike lane to turn right (merge in just before the turn), enter/exit a driveway or alley, or in some parking situations. You must yield to cyclists in the lane before entering.

questions.q: What does a triangular orange reflector on the rear of a slow-moving vehicle indicate?
opts: The vehicle is stopped and requires assistance
The vehicle is turning right
The vehicle travels at less than 25 mph — a slow-moving vehicle (SMV) marker
The vehicle is operating under a special permit
questions.exp: The SMV (Slow Moving Vehicle) emblem — a fluorescent orange triangle with a reflective red border — is required on all vehicles that typically travel under 25 mph, including farm equipment and horse-drawn vehicles.

questions.q: The safest time to pass a large truck is when you:
opts: Are alongside the truck and can see the driver in their mirror
Have completely passed the truck and can see it in your rearview mirror before moving back to the right
Are approaching the truck and the road ahead looks clear
Signal while positioned in the truck's left No Zone
questions.exp: Return to the right lane only when you can see the entire truck (including headlights) in your rearview mirror. This ensures you are fully clear and will not cut off the truck with your return maneuver.

questions.q: Two motorcycles may legally ride side-by-side in a single lane in NJ:
opts: Never — each motorcycle must occupy the full lane
Only on a highway with a speed limit of 55 mph or less
Only with police permission
Legally, but it is not generally recommended for safety reasons
questions.exp: In NJ, motorcyclists are entitled to the full use of a lane, and no motor vehicle shall deprive a motorcycle of the full use of a lane. Two motorcycles riding side-by-side (lane sharing) is generally not permitted.

questions.q: When approaching a truck that is making a wide right turn at an intersection, the safest action is to:
opts: Speed up and pass on the left before the truck begins its swing
Squeeze between the truck and the curb on the right
Wait — never attempt to pass a turning truck on either side
Honk to signal the truck driver you are there
questions.exp: Never try to pass a turning truck. The rear of the trailer tracks inside the truck's turning path and can crush a vehicle on either side. Wait until the truck has completed the turn.

questions.q: A driver who fails to yield to a blind pedestrian using a white cane in NJ faces:
opts: No penalty — pedestrian signals govern the right of way
A warning on first offense only
Significant fines and other penalties, as NJ law grants blind pedestrians absolute right of way
A minor fine similar to a parking ticket
questions.exp: NJ law specifically protects pedestrians who are blind or visually impaired. Drivers who fail to yield when a blind person is in or about to enter a crosswalk face substantial fines.

questions.q: On a road with a bicycle lane, where should you look before turning right?
opts: Only in the rearview mirror
Only in the right side mirror
In the mirror, over the right shoulder, and check for cyclists in the bike lane before turning
Only forward for pedestrians at the crosswalk
questions.exp: Before a right turn across a bike lane, check all mirrors AND physically turn to check your blind spot for cyclists. Cyclists travel faster than pedestrians and may be hidden from your mirrors.

questions.q: After an emergency vehicle with lights and siren passes, you should wait:
opts: 3 seconds before resuming normal speed
Until the driver behind you signals you to move
Until the emergency vehicle is at least 300–500 feet ahead and no other emergency vehicles are following
Exactly 30 seconds as required by law
questions.exp: Wait until the emergency vehicle is well clear (at least 300–500 feet ahead) before resuming normal driving. Multiple emergency vehicles often travel in convoy, and a second vehicle may be close behind.

questions.q: When driving near pedestrians at night, you should:
opts: Use high beams to illuminate them better
Maintain normal speed — pedestrians can see your headlights
Reduce your speed and be prepared to stop, as pedestrians are much harder to see at night
Stay in the center lane to stay away from the sidewalk
questions.exp: Pedestrians are significantly harder to see at night, even when lit by headlights. Reduce speed when in areas where pedestrians may be present. Dark clothing makes pedestrians nearly invisible.

questions.q: When sharing the road with a moped or low-speed vehicle, drivers should:
opts: Expect the moped to move to the shoulder since it is slower
Treat it the same as a bicycle
Give it the full lane and follow at a safe distance — mopeds and low-speed vehicles are legitimate lane users
Sound the horn to encourage the operator to move over
questions.exp: Mopeds and low-speed vehicles are licensed to use the road. They are entitled to the full travel lane. Pass only when it is safe to do so, giving at least 3 feet of clearance.

questions.q: What does 'sharing the road' ultimately require of drivers?
opts: Always yielding to every other road user regardless of right of way
Driving as fast as possible to minimize your impact on other road users
Recognizing and respecting the vulnerabilities of all other road users — pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, and trucks — and adjusting your behavior accordingly
Using the horn liberally to communicate your intentions
questions.exp: Sharing the road means being aware that other users are more vulnerable (pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists) or less maneuverable (trucks, buses, farm equipment) than your vehicle, and driving accordingly.
